title: Motion skills: where to extract the techniques
label: Motion skills list
summary: The skills and repositories behind the motion techniques, with licences, what each one yields and the verdict from our trial, plus a procedure for extracting a technique safely.

blocks.html:
Motion skills: where to extract the techniques

Video creation studies · Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A skill is a prompt with taste. Our skill trial found that no third-party skill beat a control built with none, and that every skill collided with the owner's rules at least once. What is worth taking is a single technique together with its evidence, and this page lists where each technique can be taken from.

Licences below were checked on the dates in the trial; they can change, so check the repository before copying anything. Verdicts are from the October 19, 2026 trial: one 39 s story, one run per skill, one auditor.

The 2D video plugin from the third tutorial (YyUP_hSovOg) is not on this list. It is handed out as a zip through a Telegram link, we did not install it, and the techniques we took from it come from measuring its demo (see Reference: 2D video plugin).

Which technique to look for where

Technique Look in
Line boil, hatching, construction lines The ProdAdvice tutorial itself; none of our studies links a public repository for it. Studio Igor's cartoon shows line boil too
Timing plan HyperFrames
Style contract ref2game (style bible), motionmaxxing (slop checklist)
Render and inspect, error log ref2game (motion checks), motionmaxxing, HyperFrames check and snapshot commands
Layered assets ref2game
One sentence, one shot herk-edit-kit (short-form-edit), claude-faceless-shorts-creator
Number readout iart-ai data-animation-skills

Rules for taking from a skill

  • Install nothing. An installed skill can change defaults silently, and copying files brings in licence terms. Keep the repositories as reading.
  • Read as data, run no code. Never run an installer or a script from a skill you have not reviewed.
  • Check the licence. AGPL and "none stated" mean reading only.
  • List conflicts first. Each skill in the trial collided with an owner rule: a moving camera, camera travel, region highlights, never-ship items.
  • Build a control. Make the same scene without the skill and let an independent check rank them by the owner's rules.
  • A checklist that demands change needs a fact to show. One checklist item pushed a builder to invent a meaning on a map; the change must use facts already in the fact table.

Skills released after October 19, 2026 and the roughly 34 downloaded repositories that were not applied have not been evaluated.

title: Motion techniques Claude can use
label: Motion techniques
summary: Twelve motion-design techniques from the studied tutorials, one article each with an animated demo of how it works.

blocks.html:
Motion techniques Claude can use

Video creation studies · Reviewed November 16, 2026

This is the practical side of the studies: each technique the tutorials describe, pulled out as its own article with a small animated demo, so an assistant (or a person) can apply it one at a time. The main source is ProdAdvice's HyperFrames tutorial (K1Mr5_7Gm3g); we add the two other tutorials the owner picked, Studio Igor's game-art experiments (YQ01D9xGAnk) and Andrey Zenin's 2D video plugin tutorial (YyUP_hSovOg).

The skills these techniques can be pulled from, with repository links, are on Motion skills: where to extract the techniques.

blocks.caption: The three groups of techniques: how the drawing looks, how the work is organised, and how picture, voice and numbers meet.

The techniques

The pencil look

Technique What it does Main source
Line boil Redraws each outline about 12 times a second while the shape stays still ProdAdvice 08:05, Studio Igor 0:49
Drawing cadence and a stable seed Keeps the drawing rhythm independent of the file frame rate, and makes a re-render identical ProdAdvice 08:22
Hatching Shades with strokes instead of a flat fill ProdAdvice 09:00
Construction lines Leaves faint guides under a contour made of short broken strokes ProdAdvice 08:05, Studio Igor 0:49

The workflow

Technique What it does Main source
Timing plan Holds every entrance, exit and path as plain numbers on one timeline ProdAdvice 01:32
Style contract Turns a look into measurable tokens that every scene shares ProdAdvice 10:14, Studio Igor 2:32
Render and inspect Checks real frames at fixed times and writes down each defect ProdAdvice 05:00, Studio Igor 20:55
Error log Turns each failure into a check for the next scene ProdAdvice 10:14, Studio Igor 14:14
Short pieces Approves scenes one at a time and reviews only the seams ProdAdvice 10:14, Zenin 6:39

Picture and voice

Technique What it does Main source
Layered assets Painted layers for forms, code for depth, light and text Studio Igor 7:48
One sentence, one shot Cuts a fraction of a second before each sentence Zenin 2:02
Number readout Shows a figure small, beside what it measures Zenin 2:26

How to use them

  1. Start from the workflow group: a timing plan and a style contract cost minutes and prevent most rework.
  2. Pick one look technique for the job and test it on one short scene. Do not stack all four of the pencil techniques on a first attempt.
  3. Run render and inspect on every scene, and keep the error log current.
  4. For narrated pieces add the picture-and-voice group.

Limits

The demos are our own drawings that show how each mechanism works. They are not frames from the tutorials, and the numbers inside them (amplitudes, spacings, pixel shifts) are illustrative unless an article says a number comes from a source. The code snippets are our proposed implementations; none of the three tutorials publishes its source. A technique that works in a demo has to be tested on a real scene, with the checks in Auditing a video, before it enters a client video.

Studies behind this page: HyperFrames tutorial study, Layered art tutorial study, Reference: 2D video plugin, Skill trial: bond Short.

title: Technique: build long work from short approved pieces
label: Short pieces
summary: Make and approve one short scene at a time, then join them and review only the seams.

blocks.html:
Technique: build long work from short approved pieces

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The creator says outright that long pieces are easier to build as smaller sections (10:14). The tutorial on a code-drawn 2D video plugin shows the same habit from another angle: it renders a pilot of about 30 s before the full video, and the author then picks one scene of the pilot to change (6:39).

blocks.caption: Four scenes of 5 s, each approved on its own, slide together into one 20 s strip. The three seams get a review flag for palette, audio and pacing.

blocks.html:
How it works

  1. Split the story into scenes of a few seconds, each with one idea. The demo uses four scenes of 5 s.
  2. Build and approve each scene alone against the style contract, with its own render and inspect pass. A defect is found in 5 s of film, not in 20.
  3. Join them into one timeline. The scenes share the palette, the seed rules and the audio bed.
  4. Review the seams. With four scenes there are three. Look at the last frame of one and the first of the next, and listen for a jump in level or ambience.

Why it helps

  • A correction touches one scene, so the others are not at risk.
  • Scenes are reusable: an approved opening can be placed in the next film.
  • A pilot gives early feedback. Render the first 8 to 10 s at draft quality and show it before the full build; after a render, send the owner a numbered sheet with one thumbnail per shot, so feedback can name a shot (see Reference: 2D video plugin).

Watch for

  • Seams. Matching colour, grain and sound level at the cut is the work that remains. A shared contract prevents most of it; the review catches the rest.
  • Scenes that cannot stand alone. If scene 3 needs scene 2 to make sense, approve them as a pair.
  • Per-scene seeds that reuse the same drawing. Two scenes with one seed will boil in lockstep. See Drawing cadence and a stable seed.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 10:14-11:41; Andrey Zenin, YyUP_hSovOg at 6:39-7:25. The 4 x 5 s split is our illustration.

title: Technique: drawing cadence and a stable seed
label: Cadence and seed
summary: Why the redraw rhythm must come from time, not from the frame number, and why the random numbers must be seeded so a re-render gives the same picture.

blocks.html:
Technique: drawing cadence and a stable seed

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Line boil needs two decisions that look like details and decide whether the effect survives a render. First, how often a new drawing appears, independent of the video's frame rate. Second, which random numbers a given moment uses, so that the same moment always looks the same.

Cadence is not the frame rate

ProdAdvice contrasts 24 and 12 fps with a ball example (08:22). The part that carries over to a production file is the idea, not the setting: the drawing rate is a look, and the file rate is a delivery format.

blocks.caption: Half a second at 12 drawings a second. The drawing rhythm stays the same; only the number of frames each drawing holds changes with the file rate.

blocks.html:
The drawing index is floor(time * 12). In a 24 fps file each drawing holds 2 frames. In a 30 fps file the holds alternate between 3 and 2 frames. Both show the same six drawings in half a second.

A seed makes a moment repeatable

A renderer may visit the same time more than once: it seeks, it re-renders a failed chunk, you scrub back to check a defect. If the outline uses a random number at every call, the second visit draws a different contour, and the defect you saw is gone or a new one appears.

blocks.caption: The same three visits to the timeline: 0.5 s, 1.0 s, then 0.5 s again. With a random number the third circle differs from the first; with a seed that comes from the scene seed plus the drawing index it is identical.

blocks.html:
The fix is one line: seed the generator with the scene seed plus the drawing index, seed = sceneSeed + floor(time * 12). Then 0.5 s is drawing 6 every time, and 1.0 s is drawing 12.

Checklist

  1. Compute the drawing index from time, never from a frame counter.
  2. Give each scene one fixed seed and store it with the scene, so a revision does not reshuffle every line.
  3. Let the camera and any text read continuous time, not the drawing index. Only the stroke follows the cadence.
  4. Do not change a required delivery rate (24, 25, 30) to imitate a source video. Keep 12 drawings a second inside the file.

This is our proposed implementation. The tutorial does not publish its code; see the source limits in HyperFrames tutorial study.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 08:22.

title: Technique: construction lines and broken strokes
label: Construction lines
summary: Leave the artist's scaffolding in the picture: faint guides under the contour, and a contour made of short strokes with gaps.

blocks.html:
Technique: construction lines and broken strokes

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A real sketch shows how it was made: a light box, a cross to find the centre, a looser first circle, then a darker contour that does not quite close. ProdAdvice lists "broken strokes" and "light construction lines" among the marks that give the handmade impression (08:05). Studio Igor's whale cartoon draws blue construction strokes before the main action (0:49).

blocks.caption: One circle in three stages: guides (a dashed box, a cross and a looser circle), then a contour of seven short strokes with gaps, then both together with the guides left faint.

blocks.html:
How it works

  • Guides go down first and in a second colour, so they read as scaffolding. A dashed bounding box, a cross through the centre and a slightly larger, looser circle are enough.
  • The contour is split into short strokes. In the demo there are seven, each ending a little before the next begins, with the end points moved by a seeded offset.
  • Together: when the contour lands, the guides drop to about half their strength (opacity 0.9 to 0.45 in the demo) and stay.

The order matters for motion. Guides appear first, which gives the eye something to track; the strokes then arrive over them. A guide that appears after the contour looks like an error.

How to build it

Treat guides as their own layer with their own opacity token. The contour function takes a stroke count and a gap size, and returns a path with several sub-paths:

const strokes = 7, gap = 0.16;   // radians left open at each seam
for (let s = 0; s < strokes; s++) {
  const a0 = (s / strokes) * TAU + gap / 2, a1 = ((s + 1) / strokes) * TAU - gap / 2;
  path.push(arc(cx, cy, r, a0, a1, jitter(seed + s)));
}

Watch for

  • Guides that compete with a label. Keep them out of the area reserved for text, or fade them out before the label arrives.
  • Gaps that look like a rendering bug. If a seam is wider than a few pixels at delivery size, reduce the gap.
  • Everything at once. Use guides on the hero object, not on every element of the frame.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 08:05-09:09, and Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk at 0:49-2:31. Stroke count, gap and opacity figures are from our demo.

title: Technique: an error log that turns into checks
label: Error log
summary: Keep a short list of concrete failures and the rule each one produced, so the next scene starts stronger without a longer prompt.

blocks.html:
Technique: an error log that turns into checks

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The last item on ProdAdvice's checklist is a list of errors (10:14). Studio Igor shows it working: when a character's hand goes behind the body while aiming upward, he adds a corrective rule to the skill (14:14). A mistake is paid for once and then guarded against.

blocks.caption: Three concrete failures and the check each produces: a label collides with the phone crop at 3.2 s (keep labels 90 px inside the safe area), hatching flips direction between frames (one angle per object, fixed seed), text flickers as the contour redraws (labels follow continuous time).

blocks.html:
How it works

Each entry has two halves:

  • What went wrong, specific enough that someone else can find it: the thing, the symptom and the time.
  • The check it becomes, a rule a script or an assistant can apply before it shows you anything.

Good entries name numbers and times. "Label collides with phone crop at 3.2 s" is useful; "text layout issues" is not. A vague entry cannot become a check.

Keep it short

Do not paste an ever-growing transcript into every prompt. Cap the log at the failures that still matter, merge entries that say the same thing, and move a rule that is always true into the style contract. Version the file with the project, so a revert brings back the matching rules.

Make it run

The best rules are tested, not just read:

if (label.box.right > frame.width - 90) fail("label inside safe area", label.id, time);

A rule that can fail loudly in the render step needs no one to remember it.

Watch for

  • Rules that fight each other. When two checks disagree, decide which wins and delete the other.
  • A log nobody feeds. Add the entry in the same sitting as the fix, while the frame number is still in front of you.
  • Rules from a different format. A check made for a map fact may not fit a character scene. Note the scope in the entry.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 10:14-11:41; Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk at 14:14-17:33. The three example entries are from our HyperFrames tutorial study and are illustrations.

title: Technique: hatching instead of a flat fill
label: Hatching
summary: Shade with strokes, not with a solid colour. A circle-and-chord recipe, a second crossing pass and the reasons it keeps a drawing from looking digital.

blocks.html:
Technique: hatching instead of a flat fill

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A flat fill is the clearest sign of a computer-made drawing. A pencil shades by laying down many short parallel strokes, and the viewer reads their spacing as light and dark. ProdAdvice shows this as a diagram that contrasts a flat fill with hatched shading (09:00).

blocks.caption: The same ball twice. Left, a flat fill. Right, diagonal strokes only on the side away from the light, then a second pass crossing the darkest part.

blocks.html:
How it works

  1. Decide where the light comes from. In the demo it is the upper left, so the shadow is on the lower right.
  2. Lay parallel strokes at one angle (45 degrees here), spaced 6 px apart, only where the surface is in shadow. Each stroke runs from one edge of the shape to the other.
  3. Add a second pass at the crossing angle over the deepest part only. Two directions read as a darker tone than one.
  4. Wobble each stroke slightly with a seeded offset (1.6 px in the demo), so the lines are not machine-straight. Draw the strokes on in order, not all at once, if the shape appears by being drawn.

How to build it

For a circle the strokes are chords. Lines x + y = k cut a circle of radius r at distance d = |cx + cy - k| / sqrt(2) from its centre, with half-length sqrt(r * r - d * d), so no clipping mask is needed. For other shapes, clip a set of long diagonal lines to the shape and keep those on the shadow side.

Spacing is the tone control. Closer strokes are darker, so a gradient of shade is a gradient of spacing, not of opacity.

Watch for

  • Hatching that changes direction between frames. Fix the angle per object and seed the offsets; see Drawing cadence and a stable seed. Put this failure in your error log.
  • Shading under text. Keep the area behind a label free of strokes, or the label loses contrast.
  • Too many strokes. A busy shape competes with the message. Reserve the dense hatch for one object.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 08:05-09:09. The chord arithmetic and the spacing values are from our demo.

title: Technique: painted layers, with light and text in code
label: Layered assets
summary: Generate the detailed pictures as separate transparent layers, then let code do depth, light, particles and text. Parallax is the proof it works.

blocks.html:
Technique: painted layers, with light and text in code

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Studio Igor's first platformer, drawn entirely in code, scored 2/10; he stopped after 37 minutes and 12 % of a weekly model allowance. His second attempt generated the pictures as images and let code move them (6:09). The split is the technique: images carry painted forms and texture, code carries scale, position, light, motion and interaction (7:48).

blocks.caption: Background, subject and foreground are images; light and text are code. Composed, a slow sideways camera moves the foreground by 18 px, the subject by 9 px and the background by 4 px (demo values) while the code layer stays still.

blocks.html:
How it works

  • Separate by depth. Generate the background, the subject and the foreground as their own layers, each on a transparent ground with room around the subject.
  • Keep mutable effects out of the pictures. Glow, shadow, particles, text and water are deliberately excluded from generated images (19:12). Draw them in code, where one number changes them.
  • Move layers by depth. When the camera shifts sideways, near layers shift more than far ones. That is parallax, and it is what makes flat pictures read as a space.
  • Hold text still. Text belongs to the code layer, so it never slides with the picture.

Check before you animate

  • Holes. When a layer moves, look for gaps at its edges. Draw layers wider than the frame, as the demo does.
  • A clean subject. Neutral light and no baked shadow, so the lighting you add does not fight the lighting in the picture.
  • A recorded source. Save each asset with its prompt, model and source reference, so a bad layer can be regenerated.

Limits

The method suits scenes and cutout characters. Studio Igor rejected AI sprite sheets and cutting one generated character into pieces; he generates separate body parts in an agreed pose and assembles them (19:12). It is not a replacement for frame animation, and the allowance percentages are one creator's account, not a transferable cost.

Details and a proposed experiment for a 5 to 10 s shot are in Layered art tutorial study. The author's open ref2game skill describes the workflow.

Source: Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk at 6:09-8:59 and 19:12-20:55. The pixel shifts in the demo are illustrative.

title: Technique: line boil, a contour that is redrawn while the shape stays still
label: Line boil
summary: Redraw each outline a dozen times a second with a little wobble, so a still pose looks hand-drawn. How it works, a small code recipe and where it goes wrong.

blocks.html:
Technique: line boil

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Hand-drawn animation never repeats a line exactly. Even a character holding still has an outline that trembles, because the artist redraws it for every drawing. Line boil copies that on purpose: the silhouette stays where it is, and only the stroke is redrawn, about 12 times a second.

blocks.caption: One circle, six drawings. On the left they play in turn, one every 83 ms, which is 12 drawings a second; on the right the same six are laid over each other. The shape does not move, only its edge does.

blocks.html:
How it works

Two things move on different clocks. The object (its position, size, rotation) follows the scene timeline smoothly. The outline of that object is a separate set of points, and those points are displaced by a small random amount, a new amount for each drawing. ProdAdvice describes exactly this for "otherwise still contours" at 12 fps (08:05), and Studio Igor's whale cartoon uses the same effect with "vibrating contours" at about 12 drawings a second (0:49).

The displacement is small. In the demo above it is 2.6 px on a circle of 62 px radius, which is about 4 % of the radius. A larger amount reads as shaking, not as pencil.

How to build it

Our own recipe, not recovered source code:

// one drawing = the same points, each moved by a seeded random offset
function boil(points, drawing, amp, sceneSeed) {
  const rand = mulberry32(sceneSeed + drawing);
  return points.map(([x, y]) => [x + (rand() - 0.5) * 2 * amp, y + (rand() - 0.5) * 2 * amp]);
}
const drawing = Math.floor(time * 12);   // the drawing cadence
draw(boil(outline, drawing, 2.6, 7));

Keep the position of the object outside this function. Pass the amplitude as one token of the style (see Style contract), so one number changes the whole film.

Watch for

  • Noise everywhere. Move only the strokes, never the labels or numbers. A label that wobbles is hard to read.
  • Too large an amplitude. If the shape seems to swim, halve the amount.
  • A drawing rhythm tied to the file. The drawing index must come from time, not from the frame number. See Drawing cadence and a stable seed.
  • Sparkle. Judge it at normal playback speed, not frame by frame. A single frame always looks fine.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g, and Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk; both are analysed in HyperFrames tutorial study and Layered art tutorial study. The amplitude figure is from our demo, not from either video.

title: Technique: a number as a readout, not a slam
label: Number readout
summary: Show a figure small, beside the thing it measures, on the spoken word, with a thin measuring line. It reads as evidence, not as decoration.

blocks.html:
Technique: a number as a readout, not a slam

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

In the demo from Andrey Zenin's tutorial, every number is an instrument readout (2:26). A thin measuring line and "50 M" stand beside a drop tower. The text is about 3 % of the frame height, not a headline.

blocks.caption: The same drop tower in two portrait frames. Left, a slam: a large "50 M" over the picture, 8 % of the frame height. Right, a readout: a thin measuring line and a small "50 M" beside the tower, 3.5 % of the frame height.

blocks.html:
How it works

  • Attach it to the thing measured. Put the label beside the object and draw the measuring line along it. The number then says what it is without a caption.
  • Make it small. In our rebuild a readout is 60 to 80 px on a 1920 px frame, which is 3.1 to 4.2 %; the drawing uses 3.5 %. The v3 bond Short set "US$8.8" as a slam of 156 px, which is 8.1 %.
  • Land it on the word. The readout arrives when the number is spoken, without a slam or a bounce.
  • One per shot, at most. The demo's other readouts are "TREMOR 0.0", "VOICE" with an even level meter and "100 %" on a popcorn bucket. Each confirms or contradicts the voice.
  • No captions and no headline type in the excerpt.

How to build it

const readout = { label: "50 M", size: 0.035 * frameHeight, at: wordStart("fifty") };

Make the label and the measuring line one component, so the line and the text always move and fade together.

Watch for

  • Unreadable on a phone. Test at arm's length. If it fails, make it slightly larger, not a slam.
  • A count-up on a ratio. Mid-count it shows a wrong ratio on screen (the bond Short builder saw "1 : 8" on the way to a different value). Show finished ratios.
  • A number the voice already says, with a label that repeats the voice. Keep a label only where the voice cannot carry the meaning.

This is a proposed change for our shorts, not an approved style rule; it was suggested in Reference: 2D video plugin and has not been audited.

Source: Andrey Zenin, YyUP_hSovOg at 2:26-2:47; Skill trial: bond Short for the count-up finding.

title: Technique: render, then inspect real frames
label: Render and inspect
summary: A quality gate that cannot be argued with: pull frames at fixed times from an actual render, write down what is wrong with each, fix the source.

blocks.html:
Technique: render, then inspect real frames

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The creator credits his model with analysing reference clips and checking its own work (05:00), and his checklist includes an agent review of frames (10:14). Studio Igor adds numbers: scripts measure foot slide, asymmetry, bone stretch and transition jolts, and image critics look at rendered frames (20:55). The shared idea is that an assistant's statement that "it looks right" is not evidence; a frame is.

blocks.caption: Frames at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 4.5 s are checked in turn. The 2.0 s frame has its label at the edge; the defect is logged with its time, the source is fixed and the clip is rendered again.

blocks.html:
How it works

  1. Render a preview of the scene, not a mock-up. A saved file is the proof that the check ran.
  2. Pull frames at fixed times: the opening, a midpoint, a transition and the last frame. For a 5 s clip that is 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 4.5 s.
  3. Write one observation per frame, with the time. "Label touches the right edge at 2.0 s" is a finding. "Looks fine" is not.
  4. Fix the source, not the frame, then render again and compare.
  5. Watch the clip once at normal speed. Frames cannot show sparkle, flicker, a missed beat or a bad hold.

A person still decides about meaning, facts and style fit. The loop removes the defects an assistant can see and hands over a short list of what remains.

Add numbers where you can

Measure what is measurable: contour displacement per frame, text bounding boxes against the safe area, the share of near-black frames. Our skill trial turned scans like these into gates, and every build failed at least one gate in a draft and was fixed before the render.

Watch for

  • A claim without a file. Require the preview path and the frame times in the report.
  • Checking only the start. Defects cluster at transitions and at the end.
  • Fixing in post. A patched frame hides a source that will break again; correct the scene.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 05:00-06:16 and 10:14-11:41; Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk at 20:55-22:50. Both describe the checks; neither publishes pass rates.

title: Technique: one sentence, one shot, cut just before the word
label: Sentence and shot
summary: Cut to a new picture a fraction of a second before its sentence begins, and put the longest pause before the punch line. Measured from a 30 s demo.

blocks.html:
Technique: one sentence, one shot, cut just before the word

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A code-drawn demo in Andrey Zenin's tutorial shows an editing grammar that carries over to any narrated video (2:02). We measured its 28.6 s excerpt with scene detection and word timestamps; the full table is in Reference: 2D video plugin.

blocks.caption: Four sentences and their four shots on a 10 s axis (illustrative times). Each cut lands 0.14 s before its sentence's first word, and the longest pause (0.8 s) comes before the punch line.

blocks.html:
What the measurement shows

  • After the first, 11 of 13 sentences get a new shot. Ten cut at the sentence start and one on the noun the shot shows. The two without a cut play out inside one held shot where the action itself changes the picture.
  • The cut comes 0.01 to 0.29 s before the first word, with a median of 0.14 s. The eye sees the new picture a few frames before the ear hears the sentence.
  • The pattern is a wide shot, then a close insert of the one detail that carries the sentence. The inserts are short (1.0 to 2.1 s); the wides carry the time (1.6 to 6.0 s).
  • Gaps between sentences run from 0.38 to 0.80 s, with a median near 0.48 s. The 0.80 s gap sits right before the punch line.
  • The camera does not travel. A closer view is a cut to a new framing, not a push.

How to build it

Mark sentence starts separately from word times in your cue file. Put shot boundaries on the sentence starts, 0.1 to 0.3 s early. Word cues inside a sentence drive reveals, not cuts.

shots = sentences.map(s => ({ cutAt: s.start - 0.14, hold: s.end }));

Give the punch line the largest gap_before value. A setup shot shows what everyone expects, a short insert shows what actually happened.

Watch for

  • Cuts inside a sentence, unless the sentence is a list.
  • A locked frame with nothing changing. A static frame is alive only if something inside it changes; our skill trial recommends a change at least every 3 s.
  • Late cuts. A cut after the word reads as lag. Keep them inside a 0.3 s window.

Source: Andrey Zenin, YyUP_hSovOg at 2:02-2:47. Measurements are ours, accurate to about 0.1 s, from the YouTube file and automatic transcription of a 30 s excerpt the author chose.

title: Technique: a style contract (style DNA) before any scene
label: Style contract
summary: Turn style words into numbers (line weight, wobble, palette, cadence) and hand them to every scene, so ten shapes look like one set.

blocks.html:
Technique: a style contract

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

"Hand-drawn" is not a style, it is a mood. ProdAdvice's checklist starts with "style DNA" and palettes (10:14). Studio Igor shows the same lesson from the other side: a generic request for pixel art fails, and the second try works because it names a 320 x 180 internal canvas, a sixfold scale and palette cycling (2:32). Later he has the agent write a "style bible" and send it with every image request (17:34).

blocks.caption: Four tokens (line 3 px, redraw 2 px, one blue, 12 drawings a second) applied to a circle, a square and a triangle, against the same three shapes with no contract: each picks its own line weight, wobble and colour.

blocks.html:
How it works

Write the contract as a short list of measurable values and keep it in one file that every scene imports:

  • Paper: background colour and texture.
  • Palette: four or fewer core colours.
  • Line: weight in pixels, and how it varies.
  • Wobble: redraw amplitude and cadence (see Line boil).
  • Shading: hatch angle and spacing (see Hatching).
  • Type and sound: the font, and the character of the sound.

Add two or three approved stills as visual anchors, and describe the mechanisms behind them in words, because a prompt that only says "like this picture" gives you a copy of the picture.

Why numbers

A token can be tested. If the contract says 3 px and a frame shows a 5 px line, that is a defect you can name. "Looks off-style" cannot be fixed by a script or by an assistant that was not in the room.

Watch for

  • Too many tokens. A contract of forty values will not be followed. Keep the ones that change the look.
  • A contract copied from someone else's film. Take the mechanisms (timing, mark types, colour relationships) and make original assets; a reference clip does not give reuse rights.
  • A contract that never changes. When a review finds a better value, update the file and re-render, not just the one scene.

In this studio a new look still goes through the style gate before client use.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 10:14-11:41; Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk at 2:32-3:37 and 17:34-19:12. The token values in the demo are ours.

title: Technique: a timing plan as editable data
label: Timing plan
summary: Write when every object enters, moves and leaves as plain numbers on one timeline, so a late correction is one edit, not a new render of everything.

blocks.html:
Technique: a timing plan as editable data

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

ProdAdvice's central claim is that a coded animation is editable: the assistant writes the graphics and the motion as code, and you change one value. A graphic on screen at 02:50 labels appearance and disappearance times, movement and colour around a common timeline (01:32-03:05). The technique is to write that plan down before any motion exists.

blocks.caption: A 5 s plan as four bars. A playhead sweeps it, then one number changes (the fact label enters at 2.4 s instead of 2.0 s) and only that bar moves; nothing else is redone.

blocks.html:
How it works

Give every object one row with its entrance time, exit time, path, scale or rotation, colour change and layer. In the demo:

Object Plan
Coastline Draws from 0 to 1 s, stays until 4.5 s
Location dot Enters at 1.0 s, stays until 4.5 s
Fact label Enters at 2.0 s (edited to 2.4 s), stays until 4.5 s
Clear Everything leaves from 4.5 s to 5.0 s

The scene reads these numbers; it does not contain them. A missed interval or a wrong coordinate is then fixed in the plan, and you do not regenerate the clip.

How to build it

Keep the plan in one object at the top of the scene file, and let every animation take its start and end from it:

const plan = {
  coast: { in: 0, draw: 1.0, out: 4.5 },
  dot:   { in: 1.0, out: 4.5 },
  fact:  { in: 2.4, out: 4.5 },
  clear: { in: 4.5, out: 5.0 },
};

Build the timeline so it can be sought: the picture at time t depends only on t and the plan, never on what played before. HyperFrames works this way with a single paused timeline (see HyperFrames build rules).

Watch for

  • Numbers hidden inside animations. If a start time lives in a tween, the plan is not the source of truth. Move it out.
  • Timing that ignores the voice. When there is narration, derive the plan from measured word times, not from guesses.
  • A plan with no end state. Always give the last object an exit, or the final frame is whatever was left over.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 01:32-03:05. The 5 s example is the exercise from HyperFrames tutorial study; the plan format is our proposal.
